content: Hello, this is a good puzzle. There are duplicate test cases, if you didn't notice.

Really good concept. I think it will be a great reverse puzzle but it needs some tweaks.

You probably want to have a minimum of 8 case pairs. The more the better for reverse, especially with so many operations to consider. I would recommend having a pair for each of the four operations where only one operation is performed so that the coder can figure out what the operations do. Alternatively, or as well, you can change the operation names to make their function more obvious. Also include case pairs with longer [[s]] strings and more operations. I would recommend lowering the constraints for n and the length of s to around 20 so that you can focus on edge cases and different combinations rather than long inputs.

I think you should turn shortest mode (and probably fastest mode) on as well since you've put in the effort to write the statement and it's a decent puzzle. On that note, I have a few recommendations for the statement.

Goal
- Avoid referring to the reader directly. The 2nd and 3rd lines can be replaced with "Given a transformed string and the operations in the order they were performed, recover the original string." or something similar. The last line could then be removed as well.

Input
- change "Lines 3 to n+2" to "Next n lines"

Constraints
- change "length(s)" to "length of s"
- make sure the constraints reflect the inputs after updating the cases
- based on the current cases, the last two lines could be replaced with "s only contains alphabetical characters"

Formatting / presentation * Please study the formatting syntax described on this page: https://www.codingame.com/playgrounds/40701/help-center/statement . Use << >> rather than and tags for bold syntax. * Please remove the headings (Goal, Input, etc.) from the individual sections. * Since this is a Reverse-mode-only clash, please add the following at the beginning of the Goal section: <> Cases * Since this is a Reverse-mode-only clash, please reorder and revise the cases so that it's possible for players to infer the task from the visible tests alone. * Please also ensure that each test and its corresponding validator cover the *same scenario* wile using *slightly different inputs and outputs*. Thanks.
Yep, fixed all of that! Updated the formatting, Reverse mode notice, and test/validator pairs. Thanks for the help!

I see that you have made some changes. It's getting better. Just to clarify, in the statement, variables (n,k,s) should be formatted as variables [[]]; constant numbers (0,1,20) should be formatted as constants {{}}. R, Lk, Bk and Xk should be formatted as constants as well, either as {{L}}[[k]] or {{Lk}}.
E.g.
{{L}}[[k]] where [[k]] is the number of positions to rotate.
{{1}} ≤ length of [[s]] ≤ {{20}}
The output section can remain unchanged. ie. <<Line 1:>> not <<Line {{1}}:>

For the case pairing, at the minimum the validator should not include any operations that were not included in the corresponding test. Ideally, for this puzzle, the only thing that would change within a pair is the string to transform.
Yeah, I sure have noticed that. I removed the duplicates and fixed the test/validator pairs. Thanks for pointing it out!

I agree that it would be better if the author could fix the current statement formatting, and I appreciate you calling this out.

That said, since only Reverse mode is currently enabled and the other modes aren't yet, I think the formatting is a relatively minor concern for now. The more important issue to address at this stage is the design of the test cases.
Thanks for the feedback! I went through the suggestions and updated the cases, statement, formatting, and constraints. Really appreciate it! ( ˶ˆᗜˆ˵ )

Test 2 and Validator 3 are the same.

Moreover, Test 2 and Validator 2 don't cover the same operations, nor do Test 3 and Validator 3.

I'd also expect slightly more small differences between the cases in each pair in terms of:
* order of operations
* value of n
* values of k
Perhaps @Sflubaduba could also comment on the clash from the player's perspective? Whether the revised cases are better now when the clash is played in Reverse mode?

My bad, I suggested that only the string change.

Luckily, I had forgotten what the operations do so I was able to give it a proper attempt. I was unable to decide what L does without the statement because it does not have its own case pair. B was also a bit difficult to lock in.

I think B would be better off as its own clash. Splitting a string by length, dealing with the overflow and reversing are all somewhat challenging alone, even in Python.

I think the operations should be given in the format required to transform the string, not the original operations performed. R, B and X are all the same reversed so figuring it out relies on L alone, and then the coder has to receive and reverse the input before following the instructions. Plus, the first 3 case pairs do not require any reversal.

X0 should probably be its own case pair because it is a decent edge case. X0 in my code was originally converting, for example, abc to cbaabc. It's difficult to pinpoint it when it's mixed in with other operations.

You could choose to keep B and the reversed operations but not make it a reverse puzzle; or change the above, add more cases and maybe change the operation names (and possibly give the operation name and value of K as separate variables).
Also, it would be best to make most of the cases use real words (either the input or output, not necessarily both). Just makes pattern recognition easier.

Extra case ideas:
 - only L (necessary)
 - only X, K=0
 - K is 2 digits for each of L, B and X
 - N is 2 digits
 - output is same as input (e.g. "abcd" -> X0+X1+R or R+R)
 - exact same operation is used multiple times
 - exact same operation is used multiple times in a row
 - K = length of S for L and B, only one operation
 - K = length of S-1 for X, only one operation
These are sound and well-founded suggestions. Would the author please consider them?
